blocks.text: Let \(f(x, y) = 0\) be any equation in two variables \(x\) and \(y\) is called a homogeneous equation of degree \(n\) (a positive integer) if the function \(f(x, y)\) is homogeneous of degree \(n\), then, \(f(kx, ky) = k^{n}f(x, y)\) for some real number \(k\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The definition sentence is garbled ('Let ... be any equation ... is called') and says 'for some real number \(k\)'. It should read: an equation \(f(x, y) = 0\) in two variables \(x\) and \(y\) is called a homogeneous equation of degree \(n\) (a positive integer) if the function \(f(x, y)\) is homogeneous of degree \(n\), that is, \(f(kx, ky) = k^{n}f(x, y)\) for every real number \(k\). ('For some \(k\)' is not enough: \(k = 1\) works for every function.)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In plain words: replace \(x\) by \(kx\) and \(y\) by \(ky\). If the whole expression just gets multiplied by \(k^{n}\), the expression is homogeneous of degree \(n\). This happens exactly when every term has the same total degree \(n\). For example \(x^{2} + 3xy\) is homogeneous of degree 2, but \(x^{2} + 3y\) is not (degrees 2 and 1).

For example, in equation (v) above if we replace \(x\) and \(y\) by \(kx\) and \(ky\) respectively, we have:
\[f(kx, ky) = k^{2}y^{2} - k^{2}(m_{1}+m_{2})xy\]
\[+\, k^{2}m_{1}m_{2}x^{2}\]
\[= k^{2}[y^{2} - (m_{1}+m_{2})xy + m_{1}m_{2}x^{3}] = 0\]
\[\Rightarrow f(kx, ky) = k^{2}f(x, y)\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book prints the last term inside the bracket as \(m_{1}m_{2}x^{3}\) and puts '\(= 0\)' after the bracket. Equation (v) has \(m_{1}m_{2}x^{2}\), and the bracket is \(f(x, y)\) itself (not 0), so the line should read:
\[= k^{2}[y^{2} - (m_{1}+m_{2})xy + m_{1}m_{2}x^{2}]\]
\[\Rightarrow f(kx, ky) = k^{2}f(x, y)\]

Thus (v) is a homogeneous equation of degree 2. A general second degree homogeneous equation can be written as: \(ax^{2} + 2hxy + by^{2} = 0\) provided \(a\), \(h\) and \(b\) are not simultaneously zero.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: How to read \(a\), \(h\), \(b\) from a question: \(a\) = coefficient of \(x^{2}\), \(b\) = coefficient of \(y^{2}\), and \(h\) = HALF the coefficient of \(xy\). For \(3x^{2} - 10xy + 3y^{2} = 0\): \(a = 3\), \(2h = -10\) so \(h = -5\), \(b = 3\). The condition 'not all zero' only rules out the empty equation \(0 = 0\).

Theorem 8: Every homogeneous second degree equation
\[ax^{2} + 2hxy + by^{2} = 0 \quad \text{...(1)}\]
represents a pair of lines through the origin. The lines are

Proof: Multiplying (1) by \(b\) and re-arranging the terms, we have:
\[b^{2}y^{2} + 2bhxy + abx^{2} = 0\]
\[b^{2}y^{2} + 2bhxy + h^{2}x^{2} - h^{2}x^{2} + abx^{2} = 0\]
\[(by + hx)^{2} - x^{2}(h^{2} - ab) = 0\]
\[\left(by + hx + x\sqrt{h^{2}-ab}\right)\times\]
\[\left(by + hx - x\sqrt{h^{2}-ab}\right) = 0\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What happened in the proof, line by line:
1. Multiplying by \(b\) makes the \(y^{2}\) term \(b^{2}y^{2} = (by)^{2}\), a perfect square to build on.
2. We add and subtract \(h^{2}x^{2}\) (total change zero). This is completing the square: \(b^{2}y^{2} + 2bhxy + h^{2}x^{2} = (by + hx)^{2}\).
3. The two leftover terms \(-h^{2}x^{2} + abx^{2} = -x^{2}(h^{2} - ab)\).
4. Now it is a difference of two squares, \(P^{2} - Q^{2} = (P + Q)(P - Q)\), with \(P = by + hx\) and \(Q = x\sqrt{h^{2}-ab}\).
The proof assumes \(b \ne 0\) (it multiplies by \(b\) and later divides by it). If \(b = 0\), equation (1) is \(x(ax + 2hy) = 0\): the lines \(x = 0\) and \(ax + 2hy = 0\), again through the origin.

Thus equation (1) represents a pair of lines whose equations are:
\[by + x\left(h + \sqrt{h^{2}-ab}\right) = 0 \quad \text{...(2)}\]
and
\[by + x\left(h - \sqrt{h^{2}-ab}\right) = 0 \quad \text{...(3)}\]

Clearly the lines (2) and (3) are (i) real and distinct if \(h^{2} > ab\) (ii) real and coincident if \(h^{2} = ab\) (iii) imaginary, if \(h^{2} < ab\). It is interesting to note that even in case the lines are imaginary, they intersect in a real point viz \((0, 0)\) since this point lies on their joint equation (1).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does the sign of \(h^{2} - ab\) decide everything? It sits under a square root.
If \(h^{2} - ab > 0\): the root is a real non-zero number, so (2) and (3) are two different real lines.
If \(h^{2} - ab = 0\): the root is 0, so (2) and (3) are the same line \(by + hx = 0\) (coincident).
If \(h^{2} - ab < 0\): the root is imaginary, so no real line exists; only the point \((0, 0)\) satisfies (1).
It is the same test as the discriminant \(B^{2} - 4AC\) of a quadratic: for \(bm^{2} + 2hm + a = 0\) (the slopes), \(B^{2} - 4AC = 4h^{2} - 4ab = 4(h^{2} - ab)\).

blocks.title: Example 16
blocks.problem: Find an equation of each of the lines represented by \(3x^{2} - 10xy + 3y^{2} = 0\).
steps:
Given: \(3x^{2} - 10xy + 3y^{2} = 0\), a homogeneous second degree equation.
To find: the equation of each of the two lines.
Method: factorize the left side by splitting the middle term. A homogeneous quadratic factorizes just like \(3t^{2} - 10t + 3\); each factor set equal to zero gives one line (zero-product rule).

Check that the lines are real
\[a = 3,\quad 2h = -10 \Rightarrow h = -5,\quad b = 3\]
\[h^{2} - ab = 25 - 9 = 16 > 0\]
Why: by Theorem 8, \(h^{2} > ab\) means two real and distinct lines, so a real factorization exists. Since 16 is a perfect square, the factors have whole-number coefficients.

Split the middle term
\[3x^{2} - 9xy - xy + 3y^{2} = 0\]
Why: we need two numbers whose product is \(3 \times 3 = 9\) and whose sum is \(-10\); they are \(-9\) and \(-1\).

Take common factors in pairs
\[3x(x - 3y) - y(x - 3y) = 0\]
Why: \(3x\) is common to the first two terms and \(-y\) to the last two; both pairs leave the same bracket \((x - 3y)\).

Factorize
\[(x - 3y)(3x - y) = 0\]
Why: \((x - 3y)\) is now common to both parts.

Separate the lines
\[x - 3y = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad 3x - y = 0\]
Why: a product is zero exactly when one factor is zero; each factor is one line through the origin.

Check:
\[(x - 3y)(3x - y) = 3x^{2} - xy - 9xy + 3y^{2}\]
\[= 3x^{2} - 10xy + 3y^{2} \;\checkmark\]
Also the slopes are \(1/3\) and \(3\): their sum \(10/3 = -2h/b\) and their product \(1 = a/b\), as Section 5.9 predicts.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: If the middle term splits easily, factorize (fastest). If it does not (surds or letters like \(\sec\alpha\)), use the ready lines (2) and (3): \(by + x(h \pm \sqrt{h^{2}-ab}) = 0\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(f(x, y) = 0\) is homogeneous of degree \(n\) when \(f(kx, ky) = k^{n}f(x, y)\): every term has degree \(n\).
2. General form: \(ax^{2} + 2hxy + by^{2} = 0\), with \(h\) = half the \(xy\)-coefficient.
3. Theorem 8: it is always a pair of lines through the origin: real and distinct if \(h^{2} > ab\), coincident if \(h^{2} = ab\), imaginary if \(h^{2} < ab\).
4. The lines are \(by + x(h \pm \sqrt{h^{2}-ab}) = 0\), or simply the two factors.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Taking \(h\) as the whole \(xy\)-coefficient: in \(3x^{2} - 10xy + 3y^{2}\), \(h = -5\), not \(-10\).
Dropping the sign of \(h\) or \(b\) when they are negative; copy the signs with the numbers.
